title: Before Serving at the Lord’s Table

sections.heading: Asking you to teach me what this meal means
sections.text: Lord, teach me to receive the Lord’s Supper as more than a religious moment. Help me see it as your gracious sign and pledge of love, given to strengthen faith. Make Christ real to me here—not because the bread and cup are magic, but because he is faithful to meet his people by his Spirit as we come to his table trusting him.
theological_themes: The Lord’s Supper as a God-given sign and pledge
Christ’s faithfulness to nourish his people
Spiritual communion with Christ by faith

scripture_references.connection: Paul speaks of the cup and bread as a real participation in Christ, not a bare reminder. This supports the prayer’s desire that Christ would make himself present to faith at his table.
Paul roots the Supper in Christ’s own command and in the proclamation of his death. The passage grounds the meal as a covenant act of remembrance and faith until Christ returns.

sections.heading: Letting the table steady my faith
sections.text: Use this meal to reassure me that your promises are not empty words. Remind me that Christ gives himself to those who receive him with thankful faith. Strengthen me so I do not drift into sin. Keep growing the life you have already begun in me, and bring it to completion when I finally see you face to face. Confirm again that I belong to you, and that you have bound yourself to me in mercy.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus identifies the bread and cup with his body given and the new covenant in his blood. This grounds the prayer’s confidence that the Supper confirms God’s covenant mercy in Christ.
Paul’s confidence is that God finishes the saving work he begins. This supports the prayer’s request that the life begun by Christ would be perfected in the end.
Jude praises God as the one able to keep his people from falling and present them blameless. That directly illuminates the prayer’s plea for strength not to fall into sin.

sections.heading: Facing the ways I have failed the people you gave me
sections.text: As I come to this feast, bring my neglect into the light. I have not cared for my own soul as I should. I have failed my family, your church, and my friends. I have held back from teaching, warning, encouraging, and setting a faithful example. I have been silent when love should have spoken. I have been careless when you called me to watchfulness.
theological_themes: Love expressed through instruction and example

scripture_references.connection: Paul charges leaders to pay careful attention to themselves and to the flock. This fits the prayer’s confession of neglect toward both personal holiness and care for others.
Paul calls Timothy to be an example and to persist in teaching and watching his life closely. This supports the prayer’s concern over failing to instruct, exhort, and model faithfulness.

sections.heading: Naming the sins underneath my silence
sections.text: Show me what has been going on inside me. I have been ignorant, not even knowing how to pray as I should. I have been spiritually dull, sometimes not delighting in speaking for you and even shrinking from it. I have been proud, refusing to say what I could say because I was afraid it would not sound good enough. I have been lukewarm, not reaching gladly for your glory. I have been lazy. I have lacked tender love. I have feared being useless, as if obedience were a waste because the seed might fall on rocky ground.
theological_themes: Confession of mixed and sinful motives
Pride, lukewarmness, sloth, and lack of love

scripture_references.connection: Paul says the Spirit helps believers in weakness when they do not know what to pray. This supports the confession of ignorance in prayer and the need for God’s help.
Paul commands Timothy to preach the word with readiness, patience, reproof, rebuke, and exhortation. This bears on the prayer’s confession of shrinking back from speaking faithfully for God.
Jesus describes seed falling on rocky ground, where the word is received only briefly. The prayer uses that image to confess fear of fruitless ministry, while still needing to obey God’s call to sow.

sections.heading: Asking you to deal with my motives, not just my actions
sections.text: Even where I have done the right thing outwardly, teach me to grieve the wrong motives that may have been underneath it. And where I have left good things undone, do not let me excuse myself. Show me when I act from pride, fear, laziness, or the desire to protect myself. Deal with those roots in me, so I can understand what obedience really requires and follow you without hiding.
theological_themes: Repentance reaching motives as well as actions

scripture_references.connection: The psalm asks God to search the heart and expose any grievous way. This grounds the prayer’s request that God reveal not only outward failures but inward motives.
Paul says the Lord will bring hidden things to light and disclose the purposes of the heart. This supports the prayer’s concern that even apparently good duties may be corrupted by wrong motives.
James teaches that knowingly failing to do good is sin. This fits the prayer’s confession of omitted duties, not merely obvious wrongdoing.

sections.heading: Coming to your table for healing and grace
sections.text: So heal me now as I come to your table. Do not let me come pretending to be whole. Meet me in my need. Fill me with your grace. Give me more than help for one duty or strength for one moment—give me yourself. Let this meal send me back to your work humbled, forgiven, strengthened, and full of love.
theological_themes: God himself as the believer’s deepest need

scripture_references.connection: Because Jesus is the great high priest who sympathizes with weakness, believers may come boldly for mercy and grace. This supports the prayer’s honest approach to God for healing and help.
Paul prays that believers would be strengthened inwardly and filled with the fullness of God. This illuminates the prayer’s final request to be filled not merely with resources, but with God himself.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original reflects a Reformed sacramental theology in which the sacrament is a seal and pledge and Christ is truly given to believers, while not implying a merely physical or automatic presence. This can be doctrinally contested among Christian traditions, so the adaptation uses language of Christ meeting his people by the Spirit and faith.

The phrase “sacramental union” is historically loaded. I rendered it as spiritual communion with Christ in the Lord’s Supper without attempting to define the mechanics beyond what the prayer itself requires.

The prayer assumes the speaker is a minister or someone with teaching and exhorting responsibilities. The adaptation preserves that setting rather than generalizing it into a prayer for any Christian.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated “guests at his table” and “as I come to the feast” as references to the Lord’s Supper, while keeping the speaker both a recipient and a servant at the table.
I interpreted “unsavouriness” as a lack of spiritual relish or delight in speaking for God, not as moral repulsiveness in a general sense.
I kept the rocky-ground image as fear that ministry may be fruitless, while framing the fear itself as something to confess rather than as a reliable judgment about whether obedience is worthwhile.

I rendered the final request, “fill me with all grace, with thyself,” as asking God not only for help but for his own presence, preserving the original’s movement from sacramental assurance to personal renewal for ministry.
